lines.text:
Catching the Train

Sara needed to travel from Manchester to London for a job interview. She decided to go by train because it was faster and more comfortable than the bus.

She bought her ticket online the night before — a return ticket, which is cheaper than buying two single tickets. She chose a specific departure time to get an off-peak fare, which costs less than a peak-time ticket.

At the station, Sara checked the departure board in the main hall. Her train was on Platform 3 and was on time. She walked through the ticket barrier by tapping her e-ticket on the reader.

The platform was busy. An announcement said: 'The ten fifteen service to London Euston is now approaching Platform 3. Please stand behind the yellow line.' Sara waited as the train pulled in and the doors opened.

She found a seat in Coach D, the quiet carriage, where passengers are asked not to use phones or play music. She put her bag on the luggage rack above her seat and sat down.

The conductor came through to check tickets. Sara showed him her e-ticket on her phone. He also reminded passengers about the next stop and the estimated arrival time.

Two hours later, the train arrived at London Euston. Sara followed the signs to the Underground and took the Tube to her interview. The whole journey had been smooth and stress-free.

lines.text: The UK rail network is one of the oldest in the world. Major operators include Avanti West Coast, LNER, and Great Western Railway. Tickets can be bought at stations, online, or via apps like Trainline.

lines.text: 'Peak' fares apply during busy commuting hours (typically 6:30–9:30 AM and 4:00–7:00 PM on weekdays). 'Off-peak' and 'super off-peak' fares are cheaper and apply outside these times. 'Anytime' tickets can be used on any train.

lines.text: In London, you can use an Oyster card or contactless bank card on the Tube and buses. 'Topping up' means adding credit to the card. Most cities now accept contactless payments for public transport.

lines.text: 'Mind the gap' is a famous announcement on the London Underground, warning passengers about the space between the train and the platform edge. It has become an iconic British phrase, appearing on souvenirs and T-shirts.
